points.title: Topology and node
points.must: Definitions of topology and node; physical vs logical topology in one line.
points.model: Topology = the layout of a network: how its nodes are connected and how data travels between them. Node = any device on a network that can send, receive or pass on data (PC, printer, server, switch, router). Physical topology = how cables and devices are laid out; logical topology = how data actually travels (a star with a hub behaves logically like a bus).

points.title: Bus topology — structure and how data travels
points.must: Labelled diagram; one backbone, terminators at both ends; data broadcast to all nodes, only the addressed node keeps it; collisions defined.
points.model: Bus: all nodes connected to one shared cable (backbone) with a terminator at each end (absorbs the signal so it does not bounce back). Data is broadcast along the backbone to every node; only the node with the matching address keeps it. Only one node can send at a time; if two send at once there is a collision and both must resend.

points.title: Bus — advantages and disadvantages
points.must: At least 2 advantages and 3 disadvantages, each with a reason.
points.model: Advantages: cheapest — least cable and no central device; easy to add a device by connecting it to the backbone; simple for small temporary networks. Disadvantages: backbone is a single point of failure — a break stops the whole network; collisions make it slow as devices/traffic increase; faults hard to locate; low security — every node receives every message; limited cable length.

points.title: Ring topology — structure and token passing
points.must: Diagram; each node connected to exactly two others in a closed loop; data in one direction through each node; token passing explained; dual ring.
points.model: Ring: each node is connected to two neighbours, forming a closed loop (no terminators). Data travels in one direction and is passed through (regenerated by) each node until it reaches the destination. Token passing: a special message (token) circulates; only the node holding the token can send, so there are no collisions and access is fair. Dual ring: two rings in opposite directions; if one link fails data wraps onto the second ring.

points.title: Ring — advantages and disadvantages
points.must: At least 2 advantages and 2 disadvantages, each with a reason.
points.model: Advantages: no collisions because of the token; steady performance under heavy load; fair, equal access for every node; no central device needed. Disadvantages: one broken cable or failed node stops the whole (single) ring; adding/removing a node disrupts the network because the ring must be opened; data passes through other nodes (delay, they handle data not theirs); faults hard to find.

points.title: Star topology — structure; switch vs hub
points.must: Diagram; each node has its own cable to a central switch; difference between hub (sends to all ports) and switch (sends only to the destination using MAC addresses).
points.model: Star: each node has its own cable to a central device; all data passes through it. Hub = copies every signal to all ports (behaves like a bus, collisions, low security). Switch = reads the destination MAC address and sends data only to that port, so it is faster (several conversations at once, no collisions) and more secure. Modern stars use switches.

points.title: Star — advantages and disadvantages
points.must: At least 3 advantages and 2 disadvantages, each with a reason; the switch as single point of failure.
points.model: Advantages: a failed cable/device affects only that device; easy to add/remove devices without disrupting others; fast and few collisions with a switch; more secure — data goes only to the destination; easy to find faults (one cable per port, port lights). Disadvantages: central switch is a single point of failure — if it fails every device loses the network; more cable than bus/ring; cost of the switch, number of devices limited by ports.

points.title: Mesh topology — full and partial
points.must: Definition; full vs partial mesh; formula n(n−1)/2 with an example; Internet as a partial mesh; wireless mesh.
points.model: Mesh: nodes connected to many (partial) or all (full) other nodes, so there is more than one route. Full mesh links = n(n−1)/2, e.g. 5 nodes → 10 links, 6 → 15, 8 → 28. Partial mesh: only important nodes have several links — the Internet is a partial mesh of routers. Wireless mesh: access points connect to each other by radio, only one needs the Internet cable.

points.title: Routing and redundancy
points.must: Definition of redundancy; data rerouted around a failed link; why banks/hospitals need it.
points.model: Redundancy = extra links or devices that provide alternative routes so the network keeps working when one fails. In a mesh each node/router chooses a route; if a link is broken or busy, data is sent another way. Needed where the network must never stop: banks (payments), hospitals, air-traffic control.

points.title: Mesh — advantages and disadvantages
points.must: At least 2 advantages and 2 disadvantages, each with a reason.
points.model: Advantages: very reliable, no single point of failure — data rerouted; carries a lot of traffic because it is spread over many links; dedicated links harder to intercept. Disadvantages: very expensive — many links (n(n−1)/2) and connections on every node; complex to set up and manage routing; much redundant cabling that is idle most of the time.

points.title: Mixed (hybrid) topology
points.must: Definition; star-bus, tree (star of stars) and star-mesh; diagram of a school with several buildings; advantages and disadvantages.
points.model: Mixed (hybrid) = combines two or more topologies. Star-bus: stars in each room joined by one backbone. Tree: core switch → switch per floor/building → star of PCs (most schools). Star-mesh: core switches/routers in a mesh, PCs in stars (banks, ISPs). Advantages: flexible — each part uses the best topology; easy to expand by adding a star; fault in one star affects only that part. Disadvantages: complex to design and manage; if the backbone/core switch fails without a spare link, several parts are cut off.

points.title: Comparison of all topologies
points.must: Table comparing bus, ring, star, mesh, mixed by cost, cable, reliability, performance, adding devices, fault finding, security.
points.model: Cost: bus lowest, ring low, star medium, mesh highest. Reliability: bus — backbone failure stops all; ring — one break stops all; star — only the switch stops all; mesh — no single point of failure. Performance: bus poor (collisions), ring steady (token), star good (switch), mesh very good. Adding devices: star easy, ring disrupts, mesh hard. Fault finding: star easy, bus/ring hard. Security: bus low (broadcast), star good with switch.

points.title: Justifying a topology for a scenario
points.must: The steps (requirements → choose → reasons applied to the scenario → disadvantage and how to manage it) and the worked computer-room example.
points.model: Steps: read requirements (devices, distance, must it never stop, budget, expansion); choose the topology whose advantages match; explain each point linked to the scenario; give a disadvantage and how to manage it. Example: 30-PC school room → star with a switch: a faulty PC/cable affects only that PC, new PCs plugged into free ports, switch keeps the room fast; full mesh would need 30×29÷2 = 435 links; keep a spare switch and a UPS.
